Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and conviction, the accused has preferred the present appeal under Sec.374(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking to set aside the same.
3. The accused in CC No.24528/2021 before the trial court has preferred the instant appeal against the complainant.

The appellant and respondent are hereby assigned with their original ranks before the trial court i.e., the appellant as accused and respondent as complainant in CC No.24528/2021 in the instant discussion for the purpose of brevity and convenience to avoid the confusion and perplexity.

4. Brief facts of the case are as follows:-
"The prosecution case, as accepted by the Trial Court, is that the complainant company is engaged in the business of sale of ready-made garments on cash and credit basis, that the accused was its customer and had purchased goods on credit during the period 2018 to 06.03.2020, that a sum of 4,12,168/- became due, and that towards discharge of the said liability the accused issued cheque bearing No.000036 dated 05.03.2020 for 4,12,168/- drawn on Bandhan Bank, Mangaluru.
The cheque, when presented through the complainant's banker, was dishonoured on 06.03.2020 with the endorsement "Funds Insufficient".
Statutory notice dated 10.03.2020 was issued and served on 13.03.2020.
The accused neither replied nor paid within the statutory period.

Hence, the complaint came to be instituted,
culminating in conviction.

The Trial Court, upon appreciating the evidence of PW-1 and the documentary exhibits Ex.P-1 to Ex.P-18(a), and after recording the statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and upon noticing the defence evidence of DW-1 with confrontation document Ex.D-1, answered all points for consideration in favour of the complainant and convicted the accused."

sentences.text: After filing of this appeal, the appellant and his learned counsel have not appeared to prosecute the appeal, despite repeated postings.
The respondent has remained represented.
The record discloses that adequate opportunities were afforded.
Yet, the appeal has not been argued either orally or by written submissions.

The Court is therefore required to decide the appeal on the basis of the trial court record and the settled principles governing appellate scrutiny in proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

7. The respondent, on the other hand, supports the impugned judgment and contends that the Trial Court has correctly drawn statutory presumptions, rightly held that the accused failed to rebut the presumption on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, and correctly imposed a compensatory sentence proportionate to the cheque amount.

8. On the basis of the materials available on record following points arise for my consideration:
1) Whether the appellant has shown "sufficient cause" within the meaning of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, for condoning the delay of 62 days in preferring the present criminal appeal?
2) Whether the appellant has made out any legal or factual ground warranting interference with the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 12.02.2025 passed in C.C. No.24528/2021?
3) What order?

9. My findings to the above points are as under:
Point No.1: In the Affirmative Point No.2: In the Negative Point No.3: As per final order for the following:
REASONS 10. Point No.1:-

The delay in preferring the present appeal is of 62 days, and the appellant has filed a separate application supported by a sworn affidavit explaining the circumstances under which the delay has occurred.

It is specifically averred that the appellant was not informed about the pronouncement of judgment by his earlier counsel, that he became aware of the conviction belatedly, and that immediately upon acquiring such knowledge, he approached the present counsel,
applied for certified copies, and thereafter proceeded to institute the present appeal.
The certified copies were supplied on 21.03.2025, and the appeal came to be filed thereafter.

The explanation, on its face, does not disclose any deliberate inaction, wilful negligence or mala fide design, but rather reflects procedural lapses and professional communication gaps which are humanly possible in the ordinary course of litigation.

11. It is now well settled that the expression "sufficient cause" occurring in Section 5 of the Limitation Act must receive a liberal and justice-oriented construction so as to advance substantial M/S Bhargav Enterprises By Naveen Rai vs M/S Bafana Clothing Co. Pvt. Ltd on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/119801313/
4 justice rather than defeat it on technical grounds.

Katiji, (1987) 2 SCC 107, has authoritatively held that refusal to condone delay results in a meritorious matter being thrown out at the very threshold and that courts must adopt a pragmatic and liberal approach while considering applications for condonation of delay.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The delay in the present case is not inordinate, and the explanation tendered appears natural and plausible, especially in the context of criminal proceedings where the right to appeal is a substantive statutory safeguard.
12. The appellant has further explained that owing to his professional commitments he was stationed at Mangaluru and could not immediately initiate appellate proceedings.

It is pertinent to note that once knowledge of the judgment was acquired, the appellant acted with reasonable promptitude by engaging the present counsel, applying for certified copies, and instituting the appeal soon after the copies were made available on 21.03.2025.
The chronology of events demonstrates continuity of effort rather than apathy, and the delay is sufficiently accounted for by circumstances beyond the immediate control of the appellant.

13. Viewed in the cumulative backdrop of the explanation offered, the length of delay, and the absence of any discernible mala fides, this Court is of the considered view that the appellant has shown "sufficient cause" within the meaning of Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Denial of condonation in such circumstances would amount to foreclosing the appellant's statutory right of appeal on hyper-technical grounds.
Accordingly, the delay of 62 days deserves to be condoned in the interest of justice.
Hence, the point No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.
14. Point No.2:-
The complainant is a company registered under the Companies Act and is engaged in the business of sale of ready-made shirts and pants on cash and credit basis.
The accused is a customer of the complainant and had purchased goods on credit during the period from 2018 to 06.03.2020.

It is the specific case of the complainant that as on the relevant date the accused was due in a sum of 4,12,168/- towards principal and contractual interest at 24% per annum in respect of nine unpaid invoices bearing Nos.12568, 11718, 11239, 11213, 11011, 10615, 10333, 9726 and 9031.
Towards discharge of the said legally enforceable liability, the accused issued cheque bearing No.000036 dated 05.03.2020 for 4,12,168/- drawn on Bandhan Bank, Mangaluru.
The said cheque, when presented through the complainant's banker, Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd., K.H. Road Branch, Bengaluru, was dishonoured on 06.03.2020 with the endorsement "Funds Insufficient".
Thereafter, statutory notice dated 10.03.2020 was issued calling upon the accused to make payment within the prescribed period, which notice was duly served on 13.03.2020.

Despite service of notice,
the accused neither replied nor made payment, thereby compelling the complainant to institute the complaint on 13.08.2020 for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

15. Upon presentation of the complaint, cognizance was taken and it was registered as P.C.R.
No.10548/2020.
Sworn statement of the complainant was recorded and, upon being satisfied that sufficient grounds existed to proceed, the matter was registered in Register No.III on 21.09.2021.
Summons was thereafter issued and the accused appeared through counsel and was enlarged on bail.
The plea of the accused was recorded, wherein he pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.

After closure of complainant's evidence, the statement of the accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded, and the accused examined himself as DW-1.

Upon appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence and after hearing arguments, the learned XXVIII Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bengaluru, by judgment dated 12.02.2025 in C.C.
No.24528/2021, convicted the accused for the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentenced him to pay a fine of 4,30,000/-, in default to undergo simple imprisonment for six months.

sentences.text: Aggrieved by the said judgment and order of sentence, the present appeal has been preferred.

16. At the outset, this Court deems it necessary to state that appellate jurisdiction in a criminal appeal is meant to correct demonstrable illegality, perversity, manifest misreading of evidence, or miscarriage of justice.
It is not an invitation to re-try the case in the abstract, nor is it a platform for speculative doubts divorced from the evidentiary record.

An appellate court interferes where the conclusions are such that no reasonable judicial mind would reach on the material available, or where the process of reasoning is vitiated by ignoring material evidence or applying wrong legal standards.
17. This Court also cannot lose sight of the nature of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
The statute, by deliberate design, introduces presumptions to uphold the credibility of negotiable instruments and to ensure confidence in commercial transactions.
Consequently, while the proceeding is criminal in form, the legislative intent makes the adjudication heavily structured around statutory presumptions, rebuttal standards, and commercial fairness.
18. In the present case, the Trial Court has recorded a clear finding that the cheque Ex.P-1 belongs to the accused and bears the accused's signature Ex.P-1(a).
The dishonour memo Ex.P-2 evidences dishonour for "Funds Insufficient".
The notice Ex.P-3 with postal receipt Ex.P-3(a) and acknowledgment Ex.P-4 establishes issuance and service.
The ledger and account material including Ex.P-5, bill-wise details Ex.P-8, invoices Ex.P-9 to Ex.P-16, and certificates under Section 65B Ex.P-17 and Ex.P-18(a) were relied upon.
These are not casual papers; they form the documentary spine of the complainant's case.
19. Once the execution of the cheque is admitted or proved, the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act springs into operation.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa v. Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441 has held that the presumption under Section 139 includes a presumption as to the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

The effect of this principle is that the complainant is not required, at the first instance, to prove the debt as if in a civil trial;
rather, the law presumes it, subject to rebuttal by the accused.
20. The rebuttal burden, though lighter than the prosecution's burden, is not illusory.
The accused must bring on record such material that, on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, renders the existence of debt or liability doubtful or improbable.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, (2019) 5 SCC 418 has lucidly explained that rebuttal can be through direct evidence or by eliciting admissions and contradictions from the complainant's evidence, but M/S Bhargav Enterprises By Naveen Rai vs M/S Bafana Clothing Co. Pvt. Ltd on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/119801313/
6 the defence must be probable, coherent, and grounded in the record.
21.

sentences.text: The primary defence projected by the accused, as noticed by the Trial Court, is that the cheque was allegedly issued as a blank security cheque and that the complainant misused it.
This Court finds that the Trial Court has addressed this defence with correct legal approach and factual reasoning.
The defence of "security cheque" is not, by itself, a talisman for acquittal.

The legal position is now well-settled that even where a cheque is issued by way of security, if it is issued in connection with a transaction and liability exists on the date of presentation, dishonour can attract Section 138.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sripati Singh (since deceased) through Gaurav Singh v.
State of Jharkhand, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1002 has reaffirmed that security cheques do not enjoy immunity where underlying liability is established.

entities.text:
Gaurav Singh v.
State of Jharkhand, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1002
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
22. The Trial Court has also relied upon the jurisprudence that even a blank signed cheque,
voluntarily handed over, attracts presumption.

In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, (2019) 4 SCC 197, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has clarified that it is immaterial who fills the particulars of a cheque, so long as the drawer's signature is admitted, and that a signed blank cheque voluntarily given would still attract the presumption under Section 139 unless rebutted by cogent evidence.

entities.text: Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, (2019) 4 SCC 197
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Likewise, in Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian, (2021) 5 SCC 283, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has reiterated that even a blank cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over, attracts the statutory presumption in the absence of credible rebuttal.

entities.text: Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian, (2021) 5 SCC 283
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 23. Measured against these binding principles, the accused's defence in the present case remains a bare assertion unsupported by contemporaneous conduct or documentary proof.

The Trial Court has correctly noticed that if the cheque were merely a security cheque and was being misused, a prudent businessman would ordinarily take immediate steps such as issuing a written demand for return of the cheque, issuing stop-payment instructions (where appropriate), lodging a complaint,
initiating civil proceedings, or at least replying to the statutory notice with a consistent defence.
The record, however, discloses that the accused did not reply to the statutory notice and did not produce any convincing material to show repayment or non-supply.
24. The accused has also alleged that the complainant did not supply goods as per invoices and that supporting documents like e-way bills were not produced.
This Court notes that the Trial Court has dealt with the evidence as it stands.
The complainant produced invoices and account statement, and PW-1 supported the transaction in oral evidence.

The accused, while contesting supply, did not produce his own account statements, payment proofs, bank entries, remittance details,
correspondence, or any commercial record that a business entity would ordinarily maintain.
A defence of "I paid everything" without a single reliable documentary trace is inherently weak in a commercial prosecution.
25. The confrontation document Ex.D-1, instead of advancing the accused's case, appears to support the complainant's ledger position as understood by the Trial Court.
The Trial Court's reasoning that Ex.D-1 reflects the outstanding and the cheque entry is not shown to be perverse.
In a case where the accused relies upon a ledger confrontation, the accused must demonstrate how that very document probabilises the defence.

Merely marking a document is not rebuttal; the defence must M/S Bhargav Enterprises By Naveen Rai vs M/S Bafana Clothing Co. Pvt. Ltd on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/119801313/
7 extract its legal consequence through credible explanation.

entities.text: Bhargav Enterprises By Naveen Rai vs M/S Bafana Clothing Co. Pvt. Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 26. On the issue of statutory notice, the accused attempted to dispute service.

The Trial Court has applied the presumption of service and has also noted that the notice was sent to the address of the accused and that there was no persuasive material to show that the address was incorrect.
The law recognises deemed service where notice is properly addressed and dispatched.
Moreover, in cheque dishonour prosecutions, the purpose of notice is to afford opportunity to pay and avoid prosecution.

Where the accused voluntarily appears before the court, contests the proceedings, and leads evidence, the plea of non-service-- without substantial proof--cannot be permitted to defeat the statutory scheme.
27.
The grounds of appeal also contain references to Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and "in charge of the business" averments.
This Court finds that, on the cause-title and the trial record as placed, the accused is the business entity represented through its authorized signatory.
The Trial Court proceedings proceeded on the footing that the drawer of the cheque was the accused's account and the accused was represented before court.

The present appeal is not argued,
and no material is placed to demonstrate that the complaint was defective for want of necessary averments in the context of the arraigned parties.

In any event, the trial culminated in a full-fledged adjudication with evidence, cross- examination, and defence evidence; at the appellate stage,
interference on such pleaded technicality requires clear demonstration of prejudice and foundational defect, which is conspicuously absent here.
28. Further, the Trial Court's approach to presumptions and rebuttal accords with the correct standard of proof.

The complainant is required to establish foundational facts such as issuance,
dishonour, notice, and non-payment.
Upon that foundation, presumption arises.
The accused then must rebut on preponderance of probabilities.
The Trial Court has repeatedly recorded that the accused produced no credible rebuttal evidence.
This Court, on independent reading, finds no misapplication of the burden of proof.
29. This Court also finds the Trial Court's reliance on the principle that mere denial or plausible explanation is insufficient to rebut the presumption to be entirely in consonance with precedent.
The accused cannot rebut a legal presumption by rhetoric.
Commercial defences must rest on commercial proof.
In proceedings under Section 138, courts are not to be swayed by conjectural pleas when the statutory presumption stands unrebutted.
30. Coming to the aspect of sentence, the Trial Court imposed a fine marginally above the cheque amount, and directed substantial compensation.
The sentence is primarily compensatory, not vindictive.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently emphasised that the object of Section 138 is to ensure credibility of instruments and to provide restitutionary relief.
The compensation ordered in the present case bears rational nexus to the cheque amount and cannot be characterised as excessive or arbitrary.
31. The appellant's conduct in the appellate proceedings also assumes significance.
The appellant invoked appellate jurisdiction and then abandoned the appeal.

The appellate court is not obliged to M/S Bhargav Enterprises By Naveen Rai vs M/S Bafana Clothing Co. Pvt. Ltd on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/119801313/
8 indefinitely adjourn a matter at the will of a litigant who does not prosecute.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bani Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (1996) 4 SCC 720 has held that a criminal appeal can be decided on merits even if the appellant or counsel is absent.

entities.text: Bani Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (1996) 4 SCC 720
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, this Court has independently examined the record and finds that even on merits, no interference is warranted.

32. In sum, the Trial Court's judgment reflects a coherent appreciation of oral and documentary evidence, correct invocation of statutory presumptions, proper analysis of rebuttal failure, and proportionate sentencing.
This Court finds neither perversity nor illegality nor any miscarriage of justice.
The grounds of appeal remain unsubstantiated, and in the absence of prosecution of appeal by the appellant, the challenge stands further weakened.
33. For the foregoing reasons, the appeal fails both on procedure and on substance.
The judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the Trial Court call for confirmation.

Therefore, Point No. 2 is answered in the Negative.
34. Point No.3

: In view of the reasons mentioned above and the findings arrived at on Point No.1 and 2, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER

The application filed by the appellant under Section 5 of the Limitation Act,
1963, seeking condonation of delay of 62 days in preferring the present criminal appeal is hereby allowed.
The delay of 62 days in filing the appeal is condoned.

The Criminal Appeal filed under under Sec.374(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 by the appellant/accused is hereby dismissed.

The Judgment of Conviction and Order of Sentence dated 12.02.2025 passed by the learned XXVIII Addl. Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bengaluru City in C.C.
No.24528/2021 is hereby confirmed.

The statute, by deliberate design, introduces presumptions to uphold the credibility of negotiable instruments and to ensure confidence in commercial transactions.
Consequently, while the proceeding is criminal in form, the legislative intent makes the adjudication heavily structured around statutory presumptions, rebuttal standards, and commercial fairness.
The accused must bring on record such material that, on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, renders the existence of debt or liability doubtful or improbable.
The defence of "security cheque" is not, by itself, a talisman for acquittal.
The legal position is now well-settled that even where a cheque is issued by way of security, if it is issued in connection with a transaction and liability exists on the date of presentation, dishonour can attract Section 138.
Commercial defences must rest on commercial proof.
In proceedings under Section 138, courts are not to be swayed by conjectural pleas when the statutory presumption stands unrebutted.
The sentence is primarily compensatory, not vindictive.
The compensation ordered in the present case bears rational nexus to the cheque amount and cannot be characterised as excessive or arbitrary.
The appellant invoked appellate jurisdiction and then abandoned the appeal.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bani Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (1996) 4 SCC 720 has held that a criminal appeal can be decided on merits even if the appellant or counsel is absent.
